items.label: f02-atomic-vs-stale
items.front: Atomic replacement and stale-write detection solve different problems. What does each one prevent?
items.back: Writing a complete temporary file and atomically moving it over the target means a reader never sees half a snapshot. It does not show whether the candidate was built from an old read; detecting that needs a comparison against what this session loaded, done under a lock.

items.front: 4: Inside the CLI, the task version check can never fail.
items.back: Options 3, 4, 6 and 7 read the task and pass its own `getVersion()` within a single command on one thread (`App.java:30-32`), so `TaskManager.expected` (`TaskManager.java:39-43`) always matches. In the two-terminal conflict, both sessions see version 1 of their own snapshot. The *file baseline* comparison (`TaskRepository.java:50`) rejects the stale one. The version check exists for adapters that hold a version across time, such as an HTTP client (Exercise 4). The unit test at `TaskWorkflowTest.java:61` exercises it by calling the service directly.

items.front: 3: An empty existing file gets an empty `.legacy-backup`.
items.back: `legacy("")` returns an empty snapshot (`TaskRepository.java:121`). The non-null, zero-byte baseline then fails the `TODOLIST1` prefix test in `save` (`TaskRepository.java:51`) and is "preserved" as a 0-byte backup (line 53). That backup then blocks any later legacy conversion to the same path with "A different legacy backup exists."

items.label: f03-lock-file
items.front: What is the tasks.txt.lock file next to the data file for?
items.back: It is the object the cooperative file lock is taken on during a save, so participating processes take turns. The app keeps it on disk; do not delete it while sessions are running. Programs that ignore the lock are not protected by it.

items.label: f01-immutable-task
items.front: Why is Task immutable, and what does an edit return?
items.back: If a manager hands out mutable tasks, a caller can change them without validation or saving. Task has only final fields; edit and withCompletion build a new Task instead of changing the old one, and the constructor re-runs all validation. The service decides whether that replacement becomes accepted state.

items.front: 1: A CRLF-converted snapshot is misdiagnosed as a broken legacy file.
items.back: `decode` sends any text not starting with exactly `TODOLIST1\n` to the legacy parser (`TaskRepository.java:107`). That parser splits on `\r?\n` and rejects the `TODOLIST1` line as a field without `=` (`TaskRepository.java:126`). Opening the file in an editor that converts it to CRLF produces `Startup stopped; existing data was not replaced. Unknown, duplicate or malformed legacy field.` with exit code 1. The data is safe, but the message sends the user to the wrong format. The source files themselves are committed with CRLF endings, which makes this mistake easy to make on Windows.

items.front: 5: The baseline is a whole-file optimistic lock.
items.back: Any accepted save by another session makes every later mutation in this session fail, even one that touches an unrelated task. `TaskWorkflowTest.java:62` shows this with two different new tasks. That is safe and simple, but under real concurrency it produces false conflicts. A SQL store with per-row versions (Exercise 5) conflicts only when two writers touch the same task.

items.front: 6: Good design worth naming: two locks, on purpose.
items.back: `FileChannel.lock()` coordinates processes, but a second lock attempt on the same file from the *same* JVM throws `OverlappingFileLockException` rather than waiting. The static `LOCAL_LOCKS` map (`TaskRepository.java:18`) serializes same-JVM callers before the file lock is taken (line 47). That keeps two `TaskManager`s in one test process from crashing each other.

items.front: 2: An oversized id leaks a Java parse message.
items.back: `selected` accepts any digit string (`App.java:43`), and `Integer.parseInt("99999999999")` throws `NumberFormatException`. That exception is a subclass of `IllegalArgumentException`, so the menu's catch (`App.java:37`) prints `Change not accepted: For input string: "99999999999"`. It is handled, but by accident.

items.explanation: The legacy format has no watermark, so legacy() computes next = max(id) + 1 = 6 and builds the snapshot with it (reproduced: "Task 6 added and saved."). From then on the TODOLIST1 header keeps the watermark.

items.prompt: A task is added (version 1), edited once, completed with option 3, then reopened with option 7. How does option 2 show it?

choices: [ ] ID 1 / v4 with the old Completed time still listed below it

items.explanation: edit and each real withCompletion change build a new Task with nextVersion(), so add, edit, complete and reopen give versions 1 to 4. Reopening passes null as completedAt, and the display adds a Completed line only for completed tasks (reproduced: "[ ] ID 1 / v4 - X2").

items.prompt: A user adds A (id 1) and B (id 2), deletes B, exits, restarts the app and adds C. Which id does C get?

choices: Id 1, as numbering starts again after every restart
Id 2, as deleted ids are put back into a free list
Id 3, from the next-id watermark saved in the file header

items.explanation: addTask takes the id from snapshot.nextId(), and encode writes that watermark on the header line next to the revision. Deleting B leaves the watermark at 3, so C is "Task 3 added and saved." (reproduced). Nothing recomputes it from the surviving ids or keeps a free list.
